title: Divisibility & remainders
examples: What is the remainder when 999999 divided by 11?
How can I find the last digit of a very large power?
Does the pattern of remainders always repeat?

explain.say: Today we look at remainders and patterns. We will learn some handy tests for divisibility. These tests help us know if one number divides another evenly.

items: Check if one number divides another evenly

explain.say: For divisibility by two, the number must end in an even digit. This means the last digit must be zero, two, four, six, or eight.

draw.text: Divisible by 2: Ends in even digit

explain.say: For divisibility by three, you must add up all the digits. If that sum is divisible by three, the whole number is too.

items: If sum is divisible by three, number is too

explain.say: Let us check the number one hundred twenty-six. The digits add up to one plus zero plus two plus six, which is nine. Nine is divisible by three, so one hundred twenty-six is divisible by three.
Next we look at the last digit of large powers. The last digits of powers often repeat in a cycle. We find this cycle length to solve big problems.

items: Last digits of powers repeat in a cycle
Find cycle length to solve big problems

faq.q: What is the remainder when a number is divided by itself?
faq.a: The remainder is always zero. This is because the number divides itself exactly, with nothing left over.
asks: What is the remainder of x divided by x?
If I divide a number by itself, what is the remainder?

faq.q: Do all divisibility tests work for every number?
faq.a: No, each test only works for specific divisors like two, three, or five. You need a different test for different numbers.
asks: Are there tests for all numbers?
Which test do I use for 7?

faq.q: How do I find the last digit of a very large power like 7 to the power of 100?
faq.a: You look for the pattern of the last digits. This pattern will repeat, and you use division to see where in the cycle the 100th position falls.
asks: What is the pattern for last digits?
How do I solve 7^100's last digit?

faq.q: Is the divisibility rule for 11 always reliable?
faq.a: Yes, the rule involves alternating sums of the digits. You add the digits in odd places and subtract the sum of digits in even places.
asks: How do I check divisibility by 11?

faq.q: What is the remainder when 100 divided by 7?
faq.a: You can divide 100 by 7. Seven goes into 100 fourteen times with a remainder of two.

facts: A number is divisible by five if its last digit is zero or five.
The remainder when dividing by a number must always be less than that number.
The last digits of powers of 2 repeat in a cycle of four: 2, 4, 8, 6.
If a number is divisible by both two and three, it must be divisible by six.

quiz.say: Is the number 435 divisible by three?

options.show: It is not possible to tell.
options.say: It is not possible to tell.

quiz.why: The sum of the digits is four plus three plus five, which equals twelve. Since twelve is divisible by three, the number is too.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the sum of the digits gives a definite answer for divisibility by three.
wrong.1: This confuses the rule for three with the rule for five.
wrong.3: This is tempting because you might only check the last digit, but the rule for three uses the sum of all digits.

quiz.say: What is the last digit of 3 to the power of 4?
quiz.why: The pattern for powers of three is 3, 9, 7, 1, which repeats. Since the exponent is 4, the last digit is the fourth in the cycle.

wrong.0: This is the last digit of 3 to the power of two.
wrong.1: This is the last digit of 3 to the power of three.
wrong.3: This is the last digit of 3 to the power of one.

quiz.say: What is the remainder when 113 divided by 4?
quiz.why: You only need to look at the last two digits, which is 13. When you divide 13 by 4, the remainder is one.

wrong.0: This is incorrect because you cannot simply subtract the divisor from the last digit.
wrong.1: This would mean the number is perfectly divisible by four, which it is not.
wrong.2: This might come from dividing the first two digits, 11, by 4.
